entries.title: The Hidden Consumer Protection Problem in AI Spending
entries.subtitle: Usage-based AI pricing lacks sufficient transparency mechanisms to enable users to predict costs before transactions, raising consumer protection and regulatory concerns.
entries.abstract: This essay examines the consumer protection implications of opaque usage-based pricing in frontier AI model APIs. While companies like Uber face budget overruns from unpredictable AI costs, users lack clear pre-transaction cost estimates despite access to pricing information through various proxies. The author argues that current pricing disclosure practices may warrant FTC scrutiny under Section 5 authority and proposes both industry-led solutions (token calculators, cost estimators) and government interventions (public workshops, guidance on transparency standards) to address information asymmetries in the AI services market.
entries.body:
The Hidden Consumer Protection Problem in AI Spending

By: S. C. Langa

Recent reports suggest that AI spending is beginning to outpace even sophisticated companies’ expectations. Uber, for example, reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 annual AI budget in only a few months. Some observers have attributed this overspending to frivolous employee use, and that may be part of the story. But it is unlikely to be the whole explanation. Companies have pushed aggressively to integrate AI into employee workflows, while many users still cannot determine how much a particular prompt, query, or task will cost before submitting it. As more frontier model providers move toward usage-based pricing, that uncertainty may become more than a budgeting inconvenience. It may become a consumer protection problem.

As it currently stands, users are given several proxies for cost, but rarely a clear estimate of cost itself. They can choose among different models, select levels of reasoning or effort, enable tools, adjust context length, and review posted token rates. Each of these choices affects the final price of a task, but none tells the user in plain terms what the task is likely to cost before it runs. Anthropic’s Claude API illustrates the problem. Its pricing materials disclose model-specific rates for input and output tokens, and its documentation separately describes features such as prompt caching, cache reads, cache writes, tool use, and extended thinking, all of which can change the final bill. Prompt caching, for example, can make repeated context cheaper, but cache creation and cache reads are priced differently from ordinary input tokens. Extended thinking can also add billable tokens that are not obvious from the user’s original prompt. OpenAI’s API follows a similar pattern: developers can select models, tools, and reasoning settings, while the company separately publishes API pricing and describes spend controls for enterprise users. These controls may be useful to engineers and administrators in some capacity, but they are not the same as a user-facing cost estimate. For someone trying to manage an AI budget, the practical question is not simply whether a rate card exists. It is whether the user can understand, in advance, the likely cost of the action they are about to take.

If these pricing practices continue and AI spending remains unpredictably variable, the consequences could extend beyond individual invoices. For consumers and enterprise customers, recurring budget overruns may translate into higher prices, reduced service quality, or new restrictions on access to AI-enabled tools. For regulators, the issue raises a familiar consumer protection question: whether users are receiving enough information to understand the cost of a transaction before they commit to it. That does not mean current pricing practices necessarily violate unfair or deceptive acts or practices law, but it does mean they may warrant closer scrutiny under the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) existing Section 5 authority. For model providers, the risk is not only regulatory. Continued confusion over AI spending could invite litigation, weaken customer trust, and push enterprise users toward competitors that offer clearer pricing controls, ultimately threatening the providers’ own bottom lines.

In order to preempt these outcomes, both government and model providers could pursue reasonable transparency measures before the problem hardens into litigation or regulation. Model providers could begin by introducing user-facing token calculators or cost estimators, similar to the tools already available for API users through providers such as Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. These tools would not need to guarantee exact prices. Their language could make clear that projected costs are estimates, while also creating a path for users to review large discrepancies between estimated and actual charges. On the government side, the FTC could convene a public workshop with enterprise users, model providers, economists, procurement experts, and researchers to better understand how usage-based AI pricing works in practice. From there, the Commission could direct staff to study whether current disclosures enable informed purchasing decisions, issue guidance on best practices for pricing transparency if warranted, and consider enforcement or recommend congressional action if evidence demonstrates substantial consumer injury or deception. Given the diversity of stakeholders in this market, the goal should not be to punish usage-based pricing itself, but to make it more intelligible, predictable, and fair.

entries.title: The Political Backlash to Data Centers
entries.subtitle: Data center opposition is rapidly growing among the public and policymakers, but proposed moratoria may be poorly targeted and create unintended regulatory consequences.
entries.abstract: This essay documents a significant shift in public opinion against data centers over the past six months, evidenced by declining polling support and increased political action at state and local levels. The author analyzes recent legislative proposals from multiple states that would impose construction moratoria or restrictions on data centers, with particular focus on New York's S9144 bill. While acknowledging legitimate concerns about grid capacity and water usage, the author argues that these moratorium bills are blunt instruments that capture non-hyperscale facilities, delegate excessive regulatory discretion to agencies without clear guidance, and fail to address the underlying policy questions about cost distribution in AI infrastructure development.

entries.title: The AI Moment? Possibilities, Productivity, and Policy
entries.subtitle: An examination of artificial intelligence adoption, productivity impacts, and implications for monetary policy in the context of historical technological transformations.
entries.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
entries.abstract: This essay by Mary C. Daly, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, analyzes the current state of AI adoption and its potential economic impacts. Drawing parallels with the century-long transformation following the discovery of electricity, the author argues that major technological changes require sustained periods of access, adoption, learning, and infrastructure development before productivity gains materialize. The piece examines what is currently known about AI's impact on the economy, identifies remaining uncertainties, and discusses appropriate monetary policy responses in both the near and long term.

entries.title: AI Model History is Being Lost
entries.subtitle: An examination of how the rapid retirement of proprietary AI models threatens historical documentation, research capabilities, and accountability in artificial intelligence development.
entries.abstract: This essay addresses the accelerating disappearance of proprietary AI models that exist only in hosted capacities, arguing that their retirement without preservation mechanisms creates significant gaps in technological history and research documentation. The author examines multiple reasons for model retirement—including legal concerns, reputational risks, and maintenance burdens—and contends that this practice reduces accountability while limiting independent research and benchmarking capabilities. The essay warns against 'technological amnesia' and advocates for greater preservation efforts to maintain historical context and enable future comparative analysis of AI development trajectories.

entries.title: Breaking the Algorithmic Contract
entries.subtitle: An exploration of the social contract framework applied to human-algorithm relationships and the surrender of curatorial autonomy to digital platforms.
entries.abstract: This excerpt from Jose Marichal's book argues that human engagement with algorithms should be understood through the lens of social contract theory, wherein users exchange curatorial autonomy for relief from decision anxiety and perceived safety. The author contends that as algorithms fail to naturally predict human behavior, humans are increasingly being conditioned to act more predictably and classify themselves according to algorithmic models. Rather than passively resisting algorithmic systems, Marichal calls for a fundamental renegotiation of the implicit socio-technical contract between individuals and technology companies.

entries.title: Section 230's Half-Bad Economics
entries.subtitle: An analysis of how Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act creates misaligned economic incentives for content moderation by digital platforms.
entries.abstract: This essay examines Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act through an economic lens, arguing that while Section 230(c)(1) appropriately assigns liability to content creators, Section 230(c)(2) distorts market incentives by shielding platforms from consequences of their own editorial decisions. The author contends that this liability protection, unlike normal business incentives, may encourage platforms to prioritize political pressures over economic efficiency. The essay considers potential solutions including common law modifications and statutory amendments, while acknowledging the political and constitutional challenges involved.

entries.title: 30 Years of Section 230: Why We Still Need It for a Safer Internet
entries.subtitle: An examination of Section 230 of the Telecommunications Act and its critical role in enabling online speech, content moderation, and internet infrastructure.
entries.abstract: This essay provides an overview of Section 230 of the 1996 Telecommunications Act, often referred to as "the 26 words that created the Internet." The piece explains Section 230's purpose in protecting online platforms from liability for user-generated content while enabling content moderation, distinguishes what the law does and does not do, and traces its legislative history stemming from the 1995 Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy case. The author argues against repealing or weakening Section 230, contending that alternative policy approaches focused on privacy, transparency, and design-based regulation offer more promising solutions to contemporary online safety concerns.

entries.title: Space Companies and Orbital Environmentalism
entries.subtitle: An argument that private sector incentives and capabilities make commercial space firms better stewards of the orbital environment than government programs.
entries.abstract: This essay challenges space environmentalists’ calls to delay private satellite launches on the grounds that large commercial networks could trigger a Kessler disaster. While acknowledging the real danger of orbital debris, it argues that activists misidentify the primary sources of space pollution and underestimate the private sector’s incentives and capacity to mitigate it. Private space firms, the essay contends, have strong financial reasons to avoid debris-generating collisions because such events would destroy their own assets and threaten future commercial activity. By contrast, public military space programs have historically created major debris fields through anti-satellite weapons testing and face strategic incentives that may encourage such behavior. The essay further argues that private companies contribute essential debris-tracking, collision-avoidance, and satellite-design technologies that reduce orbital risks while also producing substantial public benefits, including global internet access and advances in space-based manufacturing. It concludes that restricting private space activity would do little to protect the orbital environment and would instead impede innovation, making a more balanced assessment of public and private responsibility necessary for effective space policy.
entries.body:
Space Companies and Orbital Environmentalism

By: Maxwell Harden

Space environmentalists are contesting recent private sector proposals. Firms like SpaceX and Starcloud are seeking regulatory approval to launch large satellite networks containing data centers. Environmentalists are particularly concerned with the Kessler Effect, a scenario where a high number of satellites orbiting near one another means a collision would trigger a chain reaction of further collisions. These crashes would pollute Earth’s orbit with space debris, severely curtailing commercial and scientific space capabilities. Space debris, which orbits Earth at extremely high speeds, can destroy satellites and space stations. The environmentalists fear that private companies eager for profit will rapidly launch too many satellites without considering the environmental consequences of collisions. They reason that insufficiently regulated private space activities would increase the likelihood of a Kessler disaster. To support their critique, they cite several recent SpaceX satellite malfunctions that generated debris. Consequently, activists wish to delay federal approval for satellite launches.

However, space environmentalists misunderstand the sources of space debris and the solutions to space pollution. They do not consider private space firms’ low incentives for debris creation or their superior technical ability to reduce it. Addressing the environmental consequences of satellite launches requires weighing the responsibility of private versus public sector space programs in creating and managing space debris. Further, policymakers must weigh the benefits of certain space activities against the relative amounts of pollution that will inevitably be created. Private companies have a better history of preserving the space environment and the technology needed to protect it in the future. In the activists’ analysis, private space companies are not concerned with the environmental consequences of their actions and their projects will create ecological disasters in outer space. This view of orbital debris creation is wrong, and it will lead to bad policies that will not protect the space environment. 

This essay does not dispute the possibility of a Kessler disaster but rather the assumption by environmentalists that private sector companies disregard its dangers and thus require governmental supervision to avoid environmental damage. The activists misunderstand both the creation of debris and the best way to reduce it. 

First, environmentalists fail to consider the incentives of private space firms and public space programs. A Kessler scenario would be a disaster for space companies, destroying their current space assets and their future chances at innovation, growth, and success. Potential financial losses could number trillions of dollars. Debris fields that demolish their property and prevent future space launches undermine their very mission. Few people have stronger incentives to minimize orbital debris and its harms than space firms.

Alternatively, public sector efforts face mixed incentives. Space pollution poses a variety of operational challenges to certain government regulators, researchers, and scientists. These include debris collision threats to space stations and difficulties using telescopes in a crowded orbital environment. Officials at NASA, NOAA, and the FCC must account for orbital pollution, but the Pentagon is a different story. Space-focused defense programs have substantially different concerns. Anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons, which create enormous debris fields by destroying satellites, are crucial tools for modern militaries. 

Prior to an attack, war planners often seek to disable communications infrastructure in order to impede defensive responses. This strategy has evolved with technology. In the Spanish-American War, for example, American forces cut telegraph lines to Spanish colonies to prevent military coordination. Similar dynamics are at play in space conflict. For militarized public space programs like America’s Space Force or China’s People’s Liberation Army Aerospace Force (PLAASF), warfare now involves defending and attacking satellite-based telecommunications. For instance, if China were to attack Taiwan or America, they would likely start by destroying military satellites with ASAT weapons. This action would precede a broader assault and delay counterattacks by undermining military intelligence, communication, and missile targeting. Public space programs are thus heavily incentivized to develop ASAT capabilities. 

ASAT weapons testing and use threaten the space environment more than the growing number of satellite launches driven by space firms. Environmentalists concerned about private satellite launches on environmental grounds are ultimately misguided. The history of space conflict shows the reality of these incentives and fails to support the environmentalists' fears.

Government programs, not private companies, created a substantial portion of the space debris that threatens satellites and space exploration today. Specifically, Russia and China’s intentional demolitions of their own satellites as part of ASAT weapons tests created large debris fields that threaten the International Space Station. Private American space companies have not been responsible for such environmentally damaging collisions. Public space programs have weaker incentives against creating orbital debris and their own history of creating such dangerous pollution. Environmentalists will not protect the orbital environment by restricting private firms. 

Second, private space firms create the technology needed to reduce the harm of space debris. Lockheed Martin, for instance, supports the U.S. Space Force in its debris tracking efforts through its radar systems. Firms have been instrumental in mitigating the damage of space debris. Through advanced debris tracking devices like ground-based lasers or space-based sensors, companies have been able to warn each other and the International Space Station about the dangers of incoming debris. These warnings allow satellite operators to alter their orbital paths, avoiding collisions and reducing the likelihood of the Kessler Effect.

Environmentalists may note that the increasing number of satellites launched by private companies still crowds out orbital space, making accidents more likely. Even if private companies mitigate the risks of debris, large private satellite networks still do create orbital hazards each time they launch. But the private sector can also address this concern. Innovators in Japan, for instance, have tested wooden satellites that more easily disintegrate upon atmospheric reentry following their operational lifecycle. Firms have also created smaller satellites as well as protocols that allow for more satellites to be launched with less debris coming from their rockets. 

Further, private space firms provide enormous benefits to the public. Starlink satellites offer internet connectivity across the globe. Rather than building expensive infrastructure across remote areas to reach underserved populations, SpaceX can offer wireless service directly. Telecommunications are just the beginning. Space-based manufacturing may create revolutions in pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and biomedical engineering. Low gravity in Earth’s orbit means producers can create microscopic technologies more easily.

Environmental worries must accurately consider the role and incentives of space companies. Environmentalists do not recognize how the private sector promotes space environmentalism. Instead, they understate the dangers of public programs while exaggerating the harms of private firms. A balanced analysis considers not only the risks associated with new launches and projects but also the foregone benefits of not pursuing them. It is also crucial to recognize how public and private programs affect the space environment given their incentives. Environmentalists that argue for delaying launches must understand these costs and dynamics. Ignoring private sector contributions only halts future breakthroughs on the launchpad. Such a position is anti-innovation, not pro-environment.

entries.title: How Should AI Liability Work? (Part II)
entries.subtitle: An examination of how tort liability frameworks are beginning to penetrate software and AI development despite historical exemptions.
entries.abstract: This essay argues that software has historically benefited from an implicit liability wall due to the difficulty of applying traditional tort law to intangible goods and the lack of established standards of care for developers. However, this protection is eroding as courts have begun imposing liability on software companies (exemplified by Apple's battery management case and Snap's speed filter case). The author contends that AI systems, being both more powerful and more dangerous than traditional software, may accelerate this trend and force the AI community to develop proactive liability frameworks rather than awaiting legislative intervention.

entries.title: How Should AI Liability Work? (Part I)
entries.subtitle: A historical examination of how American tort liability evolved from contract-based frameworks to an expansive system of product and service accountability, with implications for AI regulation.
entries.abstract: This essay traces the development of modern American tort liability from the late 19th century to present day, examining how the legal system shifted from contract-centered responsibility assignment to broader negligence and strict liability standards. Through historical analysis and contemporary examples including the Roundup litigation, the author demonstrates how American liability law became uniquely expansive compared to other jurisdictions. The piece situates current debates about AI regulation within this longer historical context of how technocratic legal reforms produce both intended social benefits and significant unintended consequences.

entries.title: Pausing isn't policy
entries.abstract: This essay examines Senator Bernie Sanders' recent legislation proposing a federal moratorium on data center construction, arguing that while grounded in legitimate AI safety concerns, the policy approach is fundamentally flawed. The author contends that data center moratoria cannot effectively constrain AI development due to the fungibility of computing infrastructure and the global nature of AI capability buildout, citing examples from Singapore and the Middle East. Furthermore, the author argues that the moratorium's conditionsÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂencompassing labor protections, environmental standards, and export controlsÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂconstitute an overly broad policy package that conflates distinct governance challenges and represents an ineffective use of limited U.S. leverage over chip supply chains.

entries.title: Anthropic Settles Its Copyright LitigationÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂand Why That Was the Right Move
entries.abstract: This essay examines Anthropic's settlement of copyright litigation with book authors for $1.5 billion, arguing that despite the substantial payment, settling was strategically sound for the company. The analysis explains how the settlement leaves Anthropic's existing models intact while establishing a pathway for continued legal data acquisition through used book purchases. The essay contextualizes the settlement within broader copyright-AI litigation trends, compares compensation rates to industry standards, and identifies key remaining legal risks for model creators.

entries.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Architecture overview
entries.subtitle: Technical documentation explaining the Model Context Protocol's scope, core concepts, and layered architecture for context exchange between AI applications and servers.
entries.abstract: This documentation provides a comprehensive overview of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a specification for enabling AI applications to exchange context with external servers. The document outlines MCP's scope, including its specification, SDKs, development tools, and reference implementations, and explains the protocol's client-server architecture where MCP hosts establish connections to multiple MCP servers through dedicated MCP clients. The architecture consists of two layers: a data layer implementing JSON-RPC 2.0-based communication with lifecycle management and core features (tools, resources, prompts, notifications), and a transport layer managing communication channels and authentication through mechanisms such as Stdio and Streamable HTTP transport.

entries.title: What is Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)?
entries.subtitle: An open standard enabling interoperability and collaboration among siloed software agents.
entries.abstract: This explainer describes the Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), an open standard designed to facilitate agent-to-agent communication and enable interoperability across previously isolated agent systems. The document discusses how ACP can reduce integration barriers and promote collaborative agentic architectures. A prominent note indicates that ACP has been merged into the A2A standard under Linux Foundation stewardship, with the ACP team transitioning its technology and expertise accordingly, suggesting users consult official migration documentation.

entries.title: The AT Protocol Ethos
entries.subtitle: An examination of the philosophical and design principles underlying AT Protocol, a decentralized social media protocol influenced by the web, peer-to-peer, and open protocols movements.
entries.abstract: This text analyzes the foundational ethos and design principles of AT Protocol (atproto), a protocol for creating decentralized social applications. The author traces atproto's intellectual lineage to three technological movements: the document-based web with its permissionless architecture, the peer-to-peer movement's reaction against centralized platforms, and open protocol design traditions. The piece examines how atproto synthesizes these influences while introducing novel approaches to decentralized social media architecture, discussing both the innovations atproto contributes and the philosophical commitments underlying its design choices.

entries.title: What Do We Ask of Artificial Intelligence?
entries.subtitle: An examination of how societies must first determine the fundamental purpose and role of artificial intelligence systems before establishing effective governance frameworks.
entries.abstract: This essay argues that public discourse on artificial intelligence governance is disordered because it fails to address a prior fundamental question: what do we want artificial intelligence to be for us? The author identifies three broad possibilities for AI's role in society as superior reason/oracle, as reflexive tool subordinate to human knowledge, or as intermediate system stronger in narrow domains but subordinate to collective judgment. The essay contends that governance rules cannot be sensibly established without first clarifying society's intended purpose for these systems and its conception of human flourishing, drawing on philosophical and political theory to demonstrate that technological governance reflects deeper values about authority and the forms of life a society wishes to preserve.
entries.body:
What Do We Ask of Artificial Intelligence?
By: S.C. Langa

Public discourse around artificial intelligence often begins in the wrong place. We ask whether these systems should be regulated, whether they threaten jobs, whether they infringe upon intellectual property rights, and whether their underlying infrastructure places undue strain upon shared resources. These are important questions, but they all presume an earlier one that is more fundamental and far less settled: what, exactly, do we want artificial intelligence to be for us? Until that question is answered, disagreements about AI will remain disordered, because disputes over governance are often only disguised disputes over ends. A society cannot sensibly decide how to constrain a tool when it has not first decided what that tool is meant to do.

Today, at least three broad possibilities present themselves. The first is that artificial intelligence should surpass ordinary human limitations and help guide social life through superior inference, prediction, and judgment. The second is that it should remain primarily reflexive, preserving and reproducing human knowledge without occupying a higher authority than the people who made it. The third is that it should occupy an intermediate space: stronger than the individual in narrow domains, yet always subordinate to collective human judgment and political control. Each of these possibilities carries with it a different image of human flourishing, a different account of authority, and a different vision of what kind of society we are trying to build.

Before one can argue about whether artificial intelligence ought to be feared, regulated, or welcomed, one must first be clear about what is being discussed. For the purposes of this essay, artificial intelligence does not mean every digital tool, but a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from inputs how to generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, decisions, or content capable of influencing real or virtual environments (OECD; NIST). Governance, in turn, should not be understood merely as post hoc regulation, but as a broader set of legal, political, and ethical constraints through which a society directs how such systems are designed, deployed, and overseen (NIST). And if this essay asks what we want AI for, it is ultimately asking about societyÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs account of human flourishing: not efficiency alone, but what the Aristotelian tradition calls eudaimonia, or living well in the fullest sense (Kraut). Until these terms are clarified, much of the public argument about AI remains confused, because disputes that appear to concern rules often conceal a deeper disagreement about ends.

If disputes around artificial intelligence often conceal a deeper disagreement about ends, then it follows the argument that rules alone cannot settle the matter. Rules are not self-justifying. Instead, they arise from prior judgments about purpose, harm, and the forms of life a society wishes to preserve. Contemporary AI governance frameworks already reflect this logic. NIST, for example, notes that responsible AI practices help align decisions about design, development, and use with a systemÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂintended aim and values,ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ and it further explains that the identification of purposes is among the early decisions that shape later judgments about risk and even whether deployment should proceed at all (NIST 1, 23). This is not merely administrative common sense; it is a political truth. As Langdon Winner argues, technologies are not to be judged only by their efficiency or productivity, but also by the ways they can ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂembody specific forms of power and authorityÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ (121). Once that is granted, it becomes difficult to pretend that AI can be regulated sensibly before society has decided whether it wants these systems to remain instruments, become advisors, or assume some more authoritative place in human affairs. Even fear becomes unstable when purpose is left undefined, for what one person dreads as domination another welcomes as progress, and what one calls safety another calls stagnation. The disorder of public argument, then, lies not simply in disagreement over policy, but in the fact that we have too rarely said aloud what, in the first place, we want these systems to be for us.

The first and perhaps most ambitious model is that artificial intelligence ought to function as a form of superior reason: not merely as an instrument, but as a system whose predictive and inferential capacities exceed those of ordinary human beings to such a degree that it begins to resemble an oracle. On this view, the appeal of AI lies not simply in speed or convenience, but in the possibility that some forms of human error, bias, inconsistency, and ignorance might be mitigated by a more powerful intelligence. Bostrom captures the outer edge of this aspiration when he defines a superintelligence as an intellect that ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂgreatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interestÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ (22). Yet even if such a system were possible, the political question would remain unresolved. Greater intelligence is not identical with rightful rule. As Christiano notes, political authority concerns the normative power to impose duties and command obedience, not merely the possession of superior judgment (ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂAuthorityÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ). The dream of AI as superior reason therefore contains a hidden leap: it assumes that better prediction may license greater authority. That assumption is precisely what must be examined rather than smuggled in. For if, as Winner argues, technologies can embody ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂspecific forms of power and authority,ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ then the desire for an artificial oracle is not only a technical ambition but a constitutional one, since it asks whether a society is willing to vest meaningful authority in a system it did not merely build, but may come to trust more than itself (121).

The second possibility is that artificial intelligence should remain primarily reflexive, inheriting and reproducing human knowledge without claiming a higher authority than the people who made it. In this model, AI is valuable not because it transcends the human world, but because it preserves and rearticulates it at scale. Such systems would function less as oracles than as mirrors: they would organize, summarize, and recombine the language, judgments, and patterns already present in human life. There is an apparent modesty in this vision. A reflexive system may seem easier to govern precisely because it does not pretend to be sovereign. Yet its modesty is deceptive. A mirror does not only return what is best in a society; it also returns what is distorted, partial, and unjust. NISTÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs bias guidance notes that in AI systems, biases can arise from the datasets and algorithmic processes used in development, including historical and representational distortions that are already present in the social world (Schwartz et al. 8). Bender et al. make a parallel point in linguistic terms when they warn that large language models are trained to reproduce patterns in data without any grounding in meaning, making them capable of reassembling human discourse without understanding it (ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂStochastic ParrotsÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ 614). And as NobleÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs work on search demonstrates, systems that appear merely to retrieve and rank information can still reproduce and amplify existing social hierarchies rather than neutrally reflect reality (Noble). The promise of AI as mirror, then, is also its danger: a society may believe it has built something modest and familiar, only to discover that it has automated its own habits, prejudices, and limitations back onto itself.

The third possibility is that artificial intelligence should function as a form of bounded augmentation: more capable than the individual human being in narrow and useful domains, yet always constrained by human purposes, human oversight, and political judgment. This model rejects both the fantasy of artificial sovereignty and the false modesty of mere reflection. Its aim is not to create a machine that rules, nor one that simply echoes the past, but one that extends human capability while remaining answerable to human ends. There is growing support for such an approach in contemporary governance and design frameworks. The OECDÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs AI Principles insist that AI actors should respect ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂhuman-centred values and fairness,ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ including dignity, autonomy, and democratic values (OECD). NIST similarly emphasizes the need to define roles and responsibilities within ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂhuman-AI team configurationsÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ and to maintain oversight of system performance (NIST 26). From the perspective of design, Ben Shneiderman argues that well-designed systems can combine ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂhigh levels of human control and high levels of computer automation,ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ thereby increasing performance while preserving human self-efficacy, creativity, and responsibility (2). Yet the attractiveness of this middle path should not obscure its difficulty. To keep AI bounded requires more than goodwill. It requires institutions capable of deciding where automation should end, where human review must remain meaningful rather than ceremonial, and what kinds of dependence a free society ought never to permit. The question is therefore not whether bounded augmentation is appealing, but whether we possess the civic discipline required to keep it bounded.

What ultimately distinguishes these three models from one another, is not only the power they grant to artificial intelligence, but the kind of human being each one presupposes and helps produce. The question is not merely whether AI will change work, but what it will make of workers, citizens, and creators. Philosophers of labor have long argued that work matters not only because it secures income, but because it helps structure agency, social standing, and the pursuit of a meaningful life (Cholbi). From that perspective, the danger of AI is not exhausted by the prospect of unemployment. Even where labor remains, it may be thinned into supervision, correction, and procedural assent: the human being becomes less a maker than a monitor. The oracle model risks weakening judgment by encouraging deference to systems thought to know better than we do. The mirror model risks dulling creativity by returning inherited patterns in ever more polished form, making repetition easier than thought. Even the model of bounded augmentation, attractive though it is, leaves unresolved the question of responsibility, for as Mark Coeckelbergh notes, the use of AI complicates responsibility attribution even when humans remain, in principle, the responsible agents (55, 95). If human flourishing involves not simply efficiency but the exercised capacities to judge, create, answer for oneÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs actions, and participate meaningfully in a shared world, then the question of AI becomes inseparable from the question of what forms of life we are willing to let technology reorganize.

What this suggests, in the end, is that the question of artificial intelligence is fundamentally philosophical before it is technical, and civic before it is commercial. Public debate often treats AI as though its chief problems were matters of engineering capacity, market adoption, or regulatory timing. Those questions matter, but they come later. Before a society can decide how much intelligence it wants, how much automation it can tolerate, or how much risk it is willing to bear, it must first decide what ends it is prepared to order these systems toward. That is why the debate cannot be settled by benchmarks alone, nor by efficiency gains, nor by the mere fact that a technology can be built. As the OECDÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs principles insist, AI governance ultimately turns on human-centred values, fairness, dignity, autonomy, and democratic commitments (OECD). NIST similarly frames AI risk and oversight in relation to intended aims, values, and human roles rather than treating technical performance as sufficient in itself (NIST 1, 23, 26). The real difficulty, then, is not simply building powerful systems, but remaining politically and morally clear about what should guide them, what should limit them, and what must remain meaningfully human. The question of AI is therefore not only what these systems can do, but what kind of life their adoption invites us to accept.

entries.title: The Silicon Valley Canon: On the PaÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ±deia of the American Tech Elite
entries.abstract: This essay argues that Silicon Valley has a real, if informal, intellectual canon, and that the books its elites read help shape not just their ideas but their moral formation, ambitions, and sense of what kind of people ought to lead society. Framed through the classical idea of paideiaÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂeducation as the formation of characterÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂthe author contrasts WashingtonÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs narrow, credential-driven culture of expertise with Silicon ValleyÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs self-image as a world of high-agency generalists who prize intelligence, action, and sweeping first-principles thinking. He then uses a crowd-sourced list of influential tech books, from Foundation and Atlas Shrugged to Seeing Like a State, The Sovereign Individual, and Zero to One, to show how the ValleyÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂs reading habits reveal a distinctive worldview: skeptical of authority, fascinated by systems and history-making individuals, and drawn to ideas that feel both grand and actionable. It is a sharp, culturally observant piece that will especially appeal to readers interested in how the reading life of an elite class quietly shapes the politics, instincts, and blind spots of American tech power.
